thread_title: a bright white S. x wrigleyana
breadcrumb: a bright white S. x wrigleyana

posts.body_html:
Well, relatively speaking, it's not all that bright white right now, but it can produce very bright white traps during the fall. This is the result of crossing S. leucophylla var alba (mother plant) with a regular S. psittacina (pollen donor). Do a quick google search on S. x wrigleyana and you'll see most of them are red with white speckles. In contrast, this clone has the majority of its "head" "painted" in white with red veins, and much like leucophylla fall traps, this clone's most spectacular show is also during the fall. The white color can travel further down the petiole.

Here are mid to late summer traps, photo taken 8/7/15:








This thing colored up quite well last year, but it was pretty small and I never got around to snapping pix until now. Hopefully it'll put on a good show this fall.

posts.body_html:
'Chagall' is my favorite selection of x wrigleyana. The degree to which the hood stays puffed up, yet closed, makes it like a pretty little mottled balloon. And it just so happens to be naturally occurring, which is always a plus in my book. Jay mentioned it came from the extirpated Crestview radio tower site in Okaloosa Co., FL.
